first_impression.reaction: James's grandmother is Latvian and his mum keeps asking about 'the midnight thing', so I Googled it. The intro calling out the lazy 'one Baltic list' got my attention straight away. It isn't gushing and it doesn't talk down to me. The headline 'You Did Not Know?' is clickbait though, and the article is far more grown-up than that.

journey.quote: Baltic wedding traditions are usually served up as one list, as if Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius shared a single rulebook. They don't.
journey.reaction: Good. That's exactly what annoyed me about the other results. I kept reading.

journey.quote: Treat it as a fixed midnight moment in the run sheet, and ask early whether a folklore group can perform.
journey.reaction: That's actually useful. It tells me what to do about it, not just what it is. Sending this to James's mum.

journey.quote: If you want it, agree the limits beforehand.
journey.reaction: Sensible. Honestly my worry with bride stealing is the groomsmen taking it too far in front of our work friends, so I'm glad they said this.

journey.quote: During piršlybos the families met the girl's parents and agreed the economic and other terms of the marriage.
journey.reaction: Interesting history, but this stretch is quite encyclopedic. Matchmaking, dowry carriers, the return visit, and then it says they all died out over the 20th century. I skimmed it. It's not something we'd put in our day.

journey.quote: Build slack into your transfer times, and give the best man something to hand over at each gate.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of on-the-day detail I'd never think of. Exactly what I want from a planner.

journey.quote: Treat Kihnu as a living community to learn from, with local permission, rather than a backdrop.
journey.reaction: Respectful, and it saves us from being the tacky tourists. I appreciate them saying it.

journey.section: Getting married in Latvia, Lithuania or Estonia as an Australian
journey.quote: There is no Australian embassy in any of the three countries.
journey.reaction: Good to know, and the Stockholm and Warsaw detail is very specific. But the whole section is safety ratings and CNIs. Nothing about where you'd actually hold a wedding for 80 people, how guests fly in, or whether Riga in September is a realistic idea.

journey.section: Paperwork and which embassy to ask
journey.quote: For the registry steps themselves, check with the registry and the embassy, including any fees, as at November 2026.
journey.reaction: So I still have to go and work out the legal side myself? That's the bit I want someone to sort for us. It reads a bit like they're passing the buck.

journey.quote: One person is your single point of contact, and the fee and inclusions are agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: That's reassuring on hidden costs. But 'the legal and church steps stay with the registry, your church and the embassy' makes me wonder what you actually do on the legal side.

unanswered_questions: Have you planned a wedding in Riga, Vilnius or Tallinn, or a Baltic-Australian one at home? Is there a real wedding with a venue and date?
Where in the Baltics would a wedding for 60 to 90 guests actually happen, and what are the venues like?
How would you get older relatives from the airport to the venue, given there are no direct flights from Sydney?
Even if the registry has the final say, will you help us with the paperwork and chase it for us, or is that on us?
Can you find a Latvian folklore group to perform mičošana, here in Sydney or over there?
How do you handle paying local suppliers in euros, and who carries the exchange-rate risk?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Baltic Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: Clickbait headline. The article is much more grown-up than its title.

cta_reaction.quote: If you would like help shaping it, in Riga, Vilnius, Tallinn or at home, a conversation with a Wedded Advisor is a calm place to start.
cta_reaction.why: Low pressure, which I like, and the written fee is a good sign. But I've seen nothing to show they've done a Baltic wedding before, and the legal line makes me unsure how much they'd take off our plate. I'd read another post and look for a real wedding first.

top_3_changes: Add one or two insider guest-logistics lines to the 'as an Australian' section (where weddings there usually happen, the travel reality for older guests, a good season to go), so it's not only paperwork.

Say plainly what the Wedded Advisor does on the legal side (e.g. helps you gather and chase documents) while the registry decides, so 'the legal steps stay with the registry' doesn't read as 'you're on your own'.
Retitle without 'You Did Not Know?', and tighten the historic Lithuanian matchmaking and dowry sections, which read like an encyclopedia.
